result:
Two branches share no common ancestor commit. Git refuses to merge them by default (since 2.9), because joining unrelated projects is usually a mistake.

Common causes:
- Ran `git init` locally, made commits, then pulled from a remote that already had commits (e.g. GitHub-created README or LICENSE).
- Wrong remote URL: pulling a different project.
- History rewritten on one side (`git rebase --root`, `filter-branch`, orphan branch).
- Shallow clone (`--depth`) cut off the shared ancestor.

Fix depends on cause.

Both histories wanted (typical local-init-plus-remote-README case):

```
git pull origin main --allow-unrelated-histories
```

Resolve any conflicts, then commit. Same flag works on `git merge`.

Wrong remote: check with `git remote -v`, then fix with `git remote set-url origin <url>`.

Shallow clone: `git fetch --unshallow`, then retry merge.

Only remote history wanted, local commits disposable: `git fetch origin`, then `git reset --hard origin/main`. This permanently discards local commits and uncommitted changes, so confirm nothing local is needed first.

Check `git log --oneline` on both branches before using the flag. If the two histories are not meant to be one project, do not merge them.
